content: For the Scale Maternal, Newborn, and Child Health initiative, Ann Yates serves as the Lead Midwifery Advisor at the International Confederation of Midwifery, based in The Hague, Netherlands. Edgardo Abalos is the Vice Director at the Centro Rosarino de Estudios Perinatales in Rosario, Argentina. Anna Cuthbert is affiliated with Cochrane Pregnancy and Childbirth in Liverpool, United Kingdom. Virginia Diaz also works at the Centro Rosarino de Estudios Perinatales in Rosario, Argentina. Katherine Eddy is associated with the Burnet Institute in Melbourne, Australia. Leanne Jones is a Research Associate with the Cochrane Pregnancy and Childbirth Group Editorial Office at the University of Liverpool, United Kingdom. Frances Kellie is the Managing Editor of the same group at the University of Liverpool. Myfanwy Williams is another Research Associate at the Cochrane Pregnancy and Childbirth Group Editorial Office in Liverpool. The External Review Group (ERG) includes Ayse Akin from the Department of Public Health, Faculty of Medicine, Baskent University, Ankara, Turkey. Justus Hofmeyr is affiliated with the Department of Obstetrics and Gynaecology at the University of Botswana in Gaborone, Botswana, as well as the University of the Witwatersrand and Fort Hare in East London, South Africa. Tina Lavender is part of the Centre for Global Women’s Health at the University of Manchester, School of Nursing, Midwifery, and Social Work, United Kingdom. Suneeta Mittal is from the Department of Obstetrics and Gynaecology at Fortis Memorial Research Institute in Haryana, India. Alan Tita is part of the Maternal-Fetal Medicine Division and the Center for Women’s Reproductive Health at the University of Alabama at Birmingham, USA. Khalid Yunis is a Professor of Pediatrics and Head of the Division of Neonatology at the American University of Beirut, Lebanon. John Varallo is the Global Director of Safe Surgery at Jhpiego, an affiliate of Johns Hopkins University in Baltimore, Maryland, USA. WHO Country and Regional Officers include Bremen De Mucio, who focuses on Sexual and Reproductive Health at the WHO Regional Office of the Americas in Montevideo, Uruguay. Karima G. Holbzouri is based in Cairo, Egypt, at the WHO Regional Office for the Eastern Mediterranean. Chandani Anoma Jayathilaka works in Family Health, Gender, and Life Course at the WHO Regional Office for South-East Asia in New Delhi, India. Oleg K. Kuzmenko is part of the Division of Country Health Programmes at the WHO Regional Office for Europe in Copenhagen, Denmark. Leopold O. Uedraogo is involved in Reproductive, Maternal Health, and Aging at the WHO Regional Office for Africa in Brazzaville, Democratic Republic of the Congo. Howard Sobel works in Reproductive, Maternal, Newborn, Child, and Adolescent Health at the Division of NCD and Health through Life-Course at the WHO Regional Office for the Western Pacific in Manila, Philippines. Annex 1 lists external experts and WHO staff involved in the preparation of recommendations. Claudio Sosa is associated with Sexual and Reproductive Health at the WHO Regional Office for the Americas in Montevideo, Uruguay. The WHO Steering Group includes Mercedes Bonet, a Medical Officer specializing in Maternal and Perinatal Health, Sexual and Reproductive Health. Doris Chou is also a Medical Officer in the same field. Tina Lavin is a Technical Officer in Maternal and Perinatal Health. Olufemi T. Oladapo is the Unit Head for Maternal and Perinatal Health. Joshua P. Vogel is a Consultant in Maternal and Perinatal Health. Maurice Bucagu is a Medical Officer in the Maternal Health Unit. Christine Francis is a Consultant in the Department of Surveillance, Prevention, and Control. The WHO recommendation on vaginal preparation with antiseptic agents for women undergoing cesarean section aims to prevent post-operative maternal infectious morbidities. The problem addressed is the prevention of maternal infections during cesarean sections. The population of interest includes all pregnant women undergoing cesarean sections. The intervention involves vaginal preparation with an antiseptic agent, compared to no preparation or preparation with a saline solution. The setting is hospital-based, and subgroups include the type of antiseptic agent, presence of labor, and rupture of amniotic membranes. Priority outcomes include critical outcomes such as severe infectious morbidity (e.g., sepsis, septic shock, laparotomy/hysterectomy for infection, maternal ICU admission) and puerperal infection (e.g., endometritis with or without myometritis or salpingitis causing maternal febrile morbidity). Important outcomes include wound infection, side effects of antiseptics (e.g., vaginal irritation or allergy), maternal satisfaction, maternal well-being, and cost of care. These outcomes reflect updates to the 2015 WHO recommendations for preventing and treating maternal peripartum infections. The labels for severe infectious morbidity and puerperal infection have been updated to align with the current WHO definition of maternal sepsis. Evidence on the effects of vaginal preparation prior to cesarean section is derived from a Cochrane systematic review, which included 21 trials involving 7,038 women. The trials were conducted in low-, middle-, and high-income countries, including the USA, Turkey, Pakistan, Saudi Arabia, Egypt, Iran, India, Kenya, Thailand, and the UK. Fourteen trials compared iodine-based solutions to no preparation, while four trials compared chlorhexidine to no preparation. Other trials compared antiseptic solutions to saline or no washing. The interventions were described as vaginal washing, cleansing, preparation, painting, or scrubbing, and were administered using various techniques such as irrigation, gauze, sponges, or wipes. The duration of the intervention varied from 30 seconds to one minute. Some trials included women undergoing pre-labor cesarean sections, while others included women in labor or with ruptured membranes. Antibiotic prophylaxis was reported in 11 trials, with administration timing varying between before skin incision and after cord clamping. The evidence suggests that vaginal preparation with antiseptic solutions before cesarean section may not significantly reduce the incidence of maternal sepsis. However, the certainty of evidence is low. The outcomes of maternal satisfaction, well-being, and cost of care were not reported in the Cochrane review. Subgroup analyses were conducted to explore the effects of different antiseptic agents, the presence of labor, and membrane status, but these analyses should be interpreted with caution due to potential confounding factors.
